title: When a Language Falls Silent
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: There are about seven thousand languages in the world, but they are very unevenly shared. Twenty-three of them are spoken by more than half of the world's population, while thousands of others have fewer than ten thousand speakers each. Many have never been written down. According to one often-quoted estimate, a language falls silent somewhere in the world about once every two weeks, and linguists believe that around forty per cent of those still spoken are at risk of disappearing.

Languages rarely die because they are forbidden. More often they fade because speaking them stops being useful. When villagers move to cities for work, their children grow up surrounded by the dominant language, and parents who want their children to succeed at school and in the job market may decide to use it at home. The process typically takes three generations: grandparents speak the old language, their children are bilingual, and the grandchildren understand only a few words. Once children stop learning a language, its future is almost certainly short.

Why does this matter? Each language carries a store of knowledge that has built up over centuries. Dr Amara Okonjo, who has recorded the speech of elders in a forest region, found that they could name and describe the medical uses of plants for which science has no names. When the last speakers die, such knowledge goes with them. A language is also a marker of identity, and many communities that have lost theirs describe a sense of having lost the thread connecting them with their ancestors.

The first response of most linguists is documentation. They record conversations, transcribe and translate them, and compile dictionaries and grammars so that something permanent remains. Okonjo admits, though, that a recording is a kind of fossil. It preserves the sounds and the words, but a language that is no longer spoken in daily life cannot adapt to new subjects, and archives do not create speakers.

Reviving a language is far harder, but it has been done. In New Zealand, the 1980s saw the founding of Māori 'language nests', pre-schools in which elders speak only Māori to very young children. The idea spread, and within a generation the number of young people able to speak the language had risen. The most famous revival of all is Hebrew, which for centuries was used mainly in religious texts and became an everyday language again in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Few cases can be compared with it, however, since Hebrew had a long written tradition, and later the backing of a state.

Not everyone is comfortable with the language-saving movement. Professor Lena Hartmann argues that speakers have the right to choose, and that outsiders who romanticise small languages may in effect be urging poor communities to stay poor. Revival programmes, she says, succeed only when the community itself wants them. Her point deserves to be taken seriously, but it assumes that the choice is made freely, and in many places the pressure to abandon a language comes from economic necessity, and from a school system that treats it as a handicap.

Technology cuts both ways. The internet has strengthened the position of a few dominant languages, yet it also gives small communities cheap ways to teach and publish. Keyboards now exist for scripts that were once impossible to type, learning apps are available for languages with only a few hundred speakers, and researchers have found that speech-recognition software can be trained with only a few hours of recorded speech. Whether these tools will arrive in time for the most endangered languages is another matter.
